summary: Serves as the entry point to the documents about Congestion Exposure (ConEx). It explains the motivation for adding a ConEx marking at the IP layer so that information about congestion is visible to network nodes, and focuses on how this could be used. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: ConEx is a proposal for showing network devices how much congestion a sender's traffic has experienced. This information could help operators manage traffic according to its contribution to congestion.

questions: why expose congestion at the ip layer
how does conex improve traffic management
subtitle: How ConEx exposes congestion information to network devices

tldr.problem: A receiver reports congestion to a sender, but network devices along the path cannot see how much congestion a flow experienced. That limits traffic management based on each user's contribution.
tldr.mechanism: ConEx has a sender reflect congestion feedback in IP-layer packet markings. Network devices can read those markings and use them as input to traffic management.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6789 introduces the concepts and use cases for ConEx. It is informational and does not specify the protocol encoding.

facts.label: ConEx metric
facts.value: Congestion-volume: bytes dropped or ECN-marked over a period

today: RFC 6789 is an Informational document and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It introduces ConEx concepts and use cases, not a protocol encoding.

sections.title: The Congestion Information Gap
sections.content:
When network load exceeds available capacity, packets may be delayed, dropped, or marked with Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN). A receiver reports these signals to the sender, which is expected to reduce its sending rate.

RFC 6789 introduces Congestion Exposure (ConEx), which reflects congestion feedback into the IP layer. Devices along the path can then see information about congestion over the whole path. This RFC explains the motivation and possible uses; a companion document describes the abstract mechanics.
sections.plainLanguage: Today, the receiver tells the sender when packets show congestion. ConEx would also let network devices along the route see that information.

sections.title: Congestion and Congestion-Volume
sections.content:
For ConEx, congestion is measured as the probability that packets are lost or marked by ECN. The metric it exposes is congestion-volume: the volume of bytes dropped or ECN-marked during a period.

A network operator could count this volume for a user or traffic group. The RFC also defines rest-of-path congestion as the congestion a flow is expected to experience after a measurement point. A monitor can compare upstream ECN signals with whole-path ConEx signals to estimate it when the traffic and measurements support that comparison.
sections.plainLanguage: ConEx counts data that was lost or marked during congestion. A network monitor can also compare congestion already experienced with the whole-path report.

sections.title: Traffic Management Use Case
sections.content:
A network operator could place a congestion policer at an enforcement point and use ConEx markings to monitor users' congestion-volume. Like a bit-rate policer, it can apply a configured policy, but it tracks congestion contribution rather than ordinary data volume or bit rate.

When the network is not congested, the policy need not restrict traffic. During congestion, the operator could drop, delay, or lower the service class of traffic that exceeds its configured quota. The RFC presents these as possible uses, not as a required action or specified mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: An operator could use ConEx markings to identify traffic that contributes to congestion. A policy could then limit that traffic when the network is congested.

sections.title: Other Uses and Existing Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC compares ConEx with rate-based, volume-based, and application-based traffic management. Rate limits can constrain traffic when there is no congestion; volume limits count traffic regardless of congestion; and application identification can conflict with encryption and raise policy concerns.

Other proposed uses include measuring congestion between networks and informing capacity planning. The RFC also describes incentives for congestion-aware transports, but presents these as potential benefits to examine rather than established results.
sections.plainLanguage: Rate and volume limits do not directly measure congestion caused by traffic. ConEx could also help networks compare congestion or plan capacity, but the RFC treats these as possible uses.

sections.title: Deployment, Experiments, and Security
sections.content:
The RFC describes ConEx as suitable for incremental deployment: senders can mark packets, and a network can deploy policy devices without changing forwarding throughout the path. Non-ConEx packets provide no congestion report, so an operator may handle them more conservatively. The document identifies experiments needed to assess encoding choices, auditing, and deployment scenarios.

This RFC motivates the idea but does not specify a mechanism. It leaves security details to the companion document that describes the abstract ConEx protocol and its components.
sections.plainLanguage: ConEx is designed to let senders and networks adopt it in stages. This RFC describes the idea and questions for experiments, while a companion document covers mechanism and security details.
